title: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions
pub: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance, vol. 26, article 100285
author: Loukas Balafoutas · Rudolf Kerschbamer

dom.t: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess task-level legal-AI capability, lawyer–AI work allocation, verification workflows or operating-model redesign. It instead reframes digitalisation through credence-goods information asymmetry, focusing on how digital tools may both empower consumers and enable exploitation or unreliable advice.
qs: At the same time, improved access to information and the development of new digital technologies can help improve the position of consumers and restrain fraud.

st.t: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service
st.an: The review accepts the cluster’s core claim that expert-service quality depends on incentives and accountability rather than information alone, and materially develops it by showing how added information can redistribute or worsen fraud risks and by advocating context-sensitive institutional design rather than a universal remedy.
qs: Interestingly, in this equilibrium more information can be good or bad for a high-valuation consumer, depending on what the information reveals about the type of problem she has: Among high-valuation consumers, the most likely victims of cheating are those who receive a signal indicating that their problem is likely to be major, followed by the uninformed consumers and finally those who received a good signal.

We believe that a careful consideration of all of these determinants of market performance is of particular value, since it can be used as a guide for policy recommendations to devise fraud-restraining institutions and to improve efficiency.

st.t: Service necessity: Verifiability cannot ensure proper treatment
st.an: The review accepts the cluster’s core distinction between verifying what was delivered and determining whether treatment was necessary or suitable. It materially develops that proposition by showing that verifiability removes overcharging by definition but leaves mistreatment risks, performs weakly in laboratory evidence, and depends on restrictive pricing and institutional conditions.
qs: Under verifiability (but without liability) the overcharging problem is eliminated more or less by definition, but the problems of under- and overtreatment are still present.
The authors find that liability has a crucial, but verifiability at best a minor effect.

st.t: Expert matching: Observable work may remain unsuitable
st.an: The review directly supports the cluster’s proposition: expert-service customers may remain unable to assess appropriate service even after consumption; liability is more robust than verifiability; and competition can lower prices without reducing undertreatment. It also reinforces the cluster’s institution-specific qualifications rather than offering a universal remedy.
qs: Summing up this subsection, it seems fair to say that, although verifiability and liability both yield full efficiency under the specific assumptions of DK06, liability outperforms verifiability in terms of robustness – in the sense that it increases efficiency under a broader set of alternative assumptions.
Moreover, prices drop when sellers compete for buyers, but undertreatment does not decrease (and it even goes up from 53% to 73% when neither liability nor verifiability are in place).

kp.k: Expert services involve persistent informational asymmetries
kp.d: Balafoutas and Kerschbamer review theoretical and empirical credence-goods research since Dulleck and Kerschbamer (2006). Lawyers appear among the examples of experts whose customers cannot readily assess service needs or quality, including after consumption. The review concerns expert-service incentives rather than demonstrated AI-driven changes in legal employment or organisation.
qs: What do doctors, lawyers, taxi drivers, car mechanics, computer specialists and financial advisors have in common?

This is true ex ante, since the expert provider can typically observe the kind or quality of the good or service the consumer needs while the consumer cannot; but it is often also true ex post, since the consumer can often not even after consumption verify the type or quality of the service that she has received and paid for.

kp.k: Undertreatment, overtreatment and overcharging are distinct problems
kp.d: The review distinguishes insufficient services, unnecessarily sophisticated services, and billing for services not delivered. Undertreatment and overtreatment waste resources; overcharging initially transfers resources to the expert but can subsequently discourage participation, delay purchases or generate costly searches for additional opinions. In horizontally differentiated markets, inappropriate service is termed mistreatment rather than over- or undertreatment.
qs: Underprovision or undertreatment refers to the case where the service provided by the expert seller is insufficient to meet the needs of the customer.
The second problem mentioned earlier – putting a more expensive service on the bill than the one actually provided – is termed overcharging.
In a horizontally differentiated market we speak of mistreatment when the service provided does not fit to the needs of the consumer.

kp.k: Efficient pricing depends on strong institutional assumptions
kp.d: The DK06 theoretical benchmark eliminates dishonesty incentives under consumer homogeneity, commitments by both buyers and sellers, and either liability or verifiability. Liability prevents undertreatment and supports uniform prices; verifiability prevents charging for a higher quality than supplied and supports equal mark-ups. These are conditional model results, not general evidence that pricing alone eliminates expert misconduct.
qs: DK06 show that under liability (but without verifiability) the prices of the different services tend to converge to a ‘uniform price’.
DK06 show that the market will solve those problems by leading to equal mark-up prices:
If the commitment assumption is violated, then inefficiencies and fraud might arise in the market equilibrium even when liability or verifiability is in place.

kp.k: Field studies document substantial, context-specific expert misconduct
kp.d: The review reports a Swiss dental experiment in which one patient needing no treatment visited 180 dentists: 50 recommended unnecessary treatment, an overtreatment rate of 27.8%, with higher rates for low-status patients. Balafoutas et al. (2013) report approximately 45% of sampled taxi drivers taking at least a short detour and 11% overcharging. Anagol et al. (2017) find suitable life-insurance recommendations as low as 5% in their Indian audit setting. These figures describe separate markets and study designs, not a common prevalence estimate.
qs: The overall overtreatment rate is 27.8% (50 of 180 cases), and it is significantly higher for patients of low- as opposed to high socio-economic status.

Balafoutas et al. (2013) report that about 45% of the taxi drivers in their sample took at least a short detour, while 11% engaged in overcharging, requesting a higher price than the one corresponding to the distance actually driven.
The rate at which insurance agents recommend suitable products is found to be as low as 5% in this setting.

kp.k: Consumer information can protect or expose buyers
kp.d: Theoretical studies show that information indicating a serious problem can increase willingness to accept expensive recommendations and thereby invite more cheating; Schneider et al. (2016) provide supporting laboratory evidence when experts observe consumers’ information. Conversely, field studies find benefits from appearing knowledgeable: in 348 Athens taxi observations, perceived unfamiliarity with tariffs increased overcharging from 6% to 22%. In German computer repairs, a correct conjecture did not change price distributions relative to silence, while a false conjecture doubled prices.
qs: Accordingly, experts and low-risk consumers benefit from the additional information given to consumers –– at the expense of the more frequently cheated high-risk consumers.

In the charging dimension, the authors report that creating the impression of being unfamiliar with the tariff system strongly increases the likelihood of fraud in the market under consideration, from 6% to 22%.
Price distributions are indistinguishable in the first two treatments, while in the third prices double.

kp.k: Disclosure and conscientious experts can have unintended effects
kp.d: The review reports theoretical findings that commission disclosure can reduce efficiency and that the presence of honest or conscientious experts can sometimes facilitate exploitation by opportunistic experts. These mechanisms depend on model assumptions: trustworthy experts can increase customers’ acceptance of recommendations that selfish experts exploit. The authors explicitly flag Liu’s definition of overcharging as unusual. Separately, laboratory evidence on guilt aversion indicates that nonbinding promises can increase participation and reduce undertreatment and overcharging.
qs: The paper by Lowenstein et al. (2011) also suggests that disclosure can backfire, by leading to more biased advice and at the same time reducing the likelihood that such advice is turned down by consumers.

In this framework, Fong et al. (2014) examine the role of honest experts and find that the existence of honest experts increases the parameter range in which the opportunistic expert recommends dishonestly and treats inefficiently.

Such promises may refer either to the provision decision, the pricing decision, or both, and they are found to increase interaction rates by consumers and to reduce undertreatment and overcharging by experts.

kp.k: Separating diagnosis from delivery creates competing efficiency effects
kp.d: Separation removes the diagnosing expert’s direct financial benefit from selling treatment, absent collusion, but can sacrifice economies of scope. Bester and Dahm (2018) theoretically show that suitably structured contracts with separate diagnosis and provision experts can achieve first-best outcomes even with costly, unobservable diagnosis and subjective reports of success. In Greiner et al.’s (2017) laboratory experiment, separation reduced prices and overtreatment rates by 26%, increased undertreatment rates by 19%, and produced only modest, statistically insignificant efficiency gains of 5%.
qs: The idea is that the incentive to misreport the diagnosis outcome disappears if the expert cannot profit from the sale of the good.
DK06 relate the efficiency consequences of this solution to the magnitude of economies of scope between diagnosis and treatment:
As a result of the latter effect, separation is associated with only modest and insignificant efficiency gains of 5%.

kp.k: Payment systems shift overtreatment and undertreatment incentives
kp.d: The reviewed healthcare experiments consistently associate fee-for-service with greater service provision and overtreatment than capitation or fixed salaries. Capitation and salaries can instead generate efficiency losses through undertreatment. Green (2014) finds that adding a performance target does not eliminate fee-for-service overtreatment. Other experiments document altruistic motivations and substantial variation between physicians, qualifying accounts based solely on financial incentives.
qs: In general, patients tend to be subject to overtreatment under fee-for-service and to undertreatment under capitation.

Overall, a consistent pattern in this strand of the literature is that fee-for-service payment schemes lead to substantially higher rates of overtreatment compared to capitation and to fixed salaries.
On the other hand, capitation and fixed salaries also cause an efficiency loss due to higher rates of undertreatment (Hennig-Schmidt et al., 2011).

kp.k: Third-party payment can increase supplier-side fraud
kp.d: Insurance and reimbursement affect expert behaviour as well as customers’ spending incentives. In Balafoutas et al. (2017), taxi overcharging occurred in 37% of reimbursement-signalling rides versus 20% otherwise. Kerschbamer et al. (2016) report a control computer-repair price of about €70 and an increase exceeding 80% when insurance reimbursement was disclosed, principally from unnecessary parts and inflated working time. The review qualifies the welfare conclusion: insurance can also increase participation, making its overall efficiency effect context-dependent.
qs: Fraud takes the form of overcharging, which is far more likely (37% versus 20%) to occur when passengers indicate that they will be reimbursed for the costs of the ride.
In a control treatment, the average repair price is about €70, whereas the repair bill increases by more than 80% when the service provider is informed that insurance would reimburse the bill.
Therefore the overall effect of insurance on efficiency is less than obvious – depending on the circumstances it might well be positive (see Table 2 in Huck et al., 2016b, for instance).

kp.k: Liability is more robust than service verifiability
kp.d: Dulleck et al.’s (2011) 16-round laboratory markets performed substantially better under liability, whereas verifiability alone had little effect. Kerschbamer et al. (2017) explain these patterns through heterogeneous social preferences; Hilger (2016) offers a separate theoretical explanation based on customers’ inability to observe experts’ cost structures. The review concludes that liability is robust across more assumptions, while stressing implementation limits where failure is stochastic, success cannot be established independently, or extended guarantees invite consumer moral hazard. Verifiability here concerns matching charges to supplied quality, not checking AI output.
qs: The authors find that liability has a crucial, but verifiability at best a minor effect.
Third, liability is a robust institution – it performs as predicted independently of whether the seller is selfish or motivated by pro- or anti-social preferences.
Thus, a failing treatment is no perfect signal of undertreatment.
For all those reasons, liability might work better in theory than in practice.

kp.k: Competition lowers prices without reliably reducing fraud
kp.d: Dulleck et al. (2011) find that competition increases trade and lowers prices but does not ensure sufficient treatment; without liability or verifiability, undertreatment increased from 53% to 73%. Field evidence from German car repairs associates greater competition with less fraud, while Swiss dentist density did not affect overtreatment. Mimra et al. (2016a) find more undertreatment and overcharging under price competition than fixed prices, partly because lower prices reduce the returns from maintaining a good reputation.
qs: Moreover, prices drop when sellers compete for buyers, but undertreatment does not decrease (and it even goes up from 53% to 73% when neither liability nor verifiability are in place).
Based on all of the above, we sum up this subsection by saying that the impact of competition on fraud in credence goods markets is at best ambiguous.

kp.k: Reputation offers limited and inconsistent protection
kp.d: Some laboratory conditions show efficiency and overcharging improvements when consumers can reward sellers through repeat selection, but public histories do not consistently reduce fraud. Schneider’s (2012) undercover garage study found no reputational effect on treatment or charging behaviour, although diagnosis fees were approximately 37% lower when future interaction was signalled. Models also allow reputational concerns to distort otherwise appropriate recommendations, while experimental support for such negative effects is weak.
qs: The only evidence the author finds for the impact of reputational concerns is a change in the average diagnosis fee – which is approximately 37% lower when reputation matters.
Taken together, the studies discussed in this subsection fail to find a significant or particularly systematic impact of reputation and information revelation on fraud in credence goods markets.

kp.k: Second opinions help conditionally, not universally
kp.d: Agarwal et al. (2019) find laboratory improvements in diagnostic effort outcomes, correct treatment, trade and efficiency when second opinions are available, with larger efficiency benefits at lower search costs. Mimra et al. (2016b) find reduced overtreatment, but significant efficiency gains only when search costs are low. In Swiss dental field evidence, signalling an imminent second opinion reduced overtreatment only insignificantly, from 29% to 27%. Other theoretical models show that opportunities to shop elsewhere can induce experts to conceal information through mistreatment.
qs: Market efficiency increases significantly with the introduction of second opinions when search costs are low, but not when search costs are high.
The authors find no treatment difference in this respect, with overtreatment rates decreasing only slightly and insignificantly, from 29% to 27% in the second opinion condition.
There are forces that lead to less fraud and higher efficiency and countervailing forces that lead to more fraud and less efficiency.

kp.k: Diagnostic effort introduces an additional incentive problem
kp.d: The review challenges the common assumption of costless, perfectly accurate diagnosis. When effort is costly and unobservable, incentives must support both information acquisition and truthful recommendations, while preventing customers from taking advice to low-cost providers. In Dulleck and Kerschbamer (2009), efficiency requires sufficiently high search costs relative to diagnosis costs. Balafoutas et al. (2020), listed as a mimeo, theoretically and experimentally examine diagnostic uncertainty and insurance: uncertainty increases fraudulent provision and reduces entry, lowering efficiency by about 16%; insurance also reduces investment in precision.
qs: Under verifiability, solving problem (ii) requires equal mark-up prices; but with equal mark-ups (and no other forces pushing towards honesty) experts have no incentives to invest in diagnosis.
Diagnostic uncertainty not only increases fraudulent provision rates, but it also reduces market entry rates by consumers.
These effects combined have a strong negative impact on efficiency, reducing it by about 16%.

kp.k: Fair prices signal expert characteristics rather than cause honesty
kp.d: Dulleck et al. (2012) investigate whether fair prices induce better service or instead reflect sellers’ preferences. Experimental comparisons between seller-chosen and externally imposed prices support the latter explanation: associations between fair prices and efficient treatment disappear with expert fixed effects or exogenous prices. The review cautions that price regulation could remove information about seller type. Separately, Balafoutas et al. (2015) find lower efficiency when either contracting party reveals tax dishonesty than when both are tax-honest.
qs: Thus, it is not the case that fair prices induce good behavior; instead, good experts frequently choose fair prices.
when at least one of the contracting parties (the buyer or the seller) is tax-dishonest, efficiency is substantially lower compared to the situation in which two tax-honest agents interact.

kp.k: Digital information creates opportunities requiring further research
kp.d: The authors propose that digital tools may improve consumers’ position through GPS navigation, online information, algorithmic medical advice and expert-review platforms, and note comparable advice tools for legal, financial and insurance services. They explicitly caution against dubious online medical information and frame digitalisation’s effects as a future research agenda, not established evidence of AI transforming legal work. They also distinguish classical credence goods, concerning suitability for a consumer, from label credence goods, concerning unobservable product attributes, for which different remedies are relevant.
qs: At the same time, improved access to information and the development of new digital technologies can help improve the position of consumers and restrain fraud.
Similar kinds of tools are available to customers seeking advice regarding financial, legal or insurance services.

We believe it is important to shed light into the way that digitalization and new technologies are likely to affect credence goods in the present and future and hold this to be an exciting and promising avenue for future research.
In this alternative definition the asymmetric information concerns the characteristics of the good, and not its suitability for a particular consumer.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Balafoutas and Kerschbamer argue that digital information and advice technologies can strengthen consumers’ position and restrain fraud in expert-service markets.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain review of credence goods, not an analysis of AI-driven legal-sector transformation. In their conclusion, the authors identify online medical advice supplied by doctors or algorithmic robots and state that similar tools are available for financial, legal and insurance advice. They also suggest that online reviews can help consumers learn about individual experts and potentially reduce fraud through competition and reputation. They do not predict lawyer displacement, changes in legal staffing, or quantified legal-service productivity gains.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology claims are qualitative observations and a research outlook, rather than findings from AI or legal-service evaluations.
pts.d: The authors illustrate the potential benefits with GPS-assisted taxi passengers, online medical advice and online review platforms. The review supplies theoretical, laboratory and field evidence about information and incentives, but no direct measurement of AI’s effects on legal services. Relevant evidence also qualifies the optimistic outlook: the reviewed computer-repair field experiment by Kerschbamer et al. (2019) found that voicing a false diagnosis doubled prices, whereas correct conjectures produced prices indistinguishable from saying nothing. The review’s broader evidence does not establish a systematic fraud-reducing effect of reputation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The authors describe technologies available in 2020 and possible continuing benefits, without specifying an adoption deadline or magnitude of change.
pts.d: The review version is dated February 1, 2020. Its conclusion presents digital tools as already available, while treating their effects as an avenue for future research. Benefits are conditional rather than guaranteed: consumers need access to useful information, and unreliable internet advice can be harmful. The authors’ summaries of competition, reputation and second-opinion research further caution against interpreting improved information access as an automatic cure for fraud.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries envisaged are consumers of expert services, including people seeking legal advice.
pts.d: The authors discuss taxi passengers, patients, and customers seeking financial, legal or insurance advice. Digital tools may help them understand their needs and assess providers, reducing their informational disadvantage. Expert sellers may consequently face stronger scrutiny and competitive or reputational incentives. Legal advice is explicitly included, but the source does not distinguish corporate clients from individuals, identify affected law-firm segments, or describe changes to lawyers’ work.
